# How to use this editorial

For each task, stop after the first block that repairs your attempt. The
proof is part of the solution: at the advanced gates, recognizing a data
structure without proving the reduction is not enough.

# 1. ABC083_B -- Some Sums (approximately 100)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc083/tasks/abc083_b?lang=en>

## Restatement

Given N, A, and B, sum every integer x in 1..N whose decimal digit sum lies in the inclusive interval [A,B]. The bounds are small enough to inspect every candidate.

## Recognition and derivation

Enumerate x and compute its digit sum by repeatedly taking x % 10 and dividing by 10. Add the original x exactly when the sum is in [A,B]. This is the deliberately short entry ramp.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Every eligible integer is visited once, and the test is exactly the definition of eligibility; therefore the accumulator contains all and only required integers.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N log N) time and O(1) auxiliary memory. The interval is inclusive, and the number added is x, not its digit sum.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 2. ABC210_C -- Colorful Candies (approximately 400)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc210/tasks/abc210_c?lang=en>

## Restatement

Given N candy colors and a window length K, find the maximum number of distinct colors in any K consecutive positions.

## Recognition and derivation

Maintain a frequency map for the current fixed-length window. When the right endpoint advances, insert the entering color and erase the leaving color if its count becomes zero. Track the map size.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

After each update the map stores exactly the multiplicity of every color in the current K positions, so its number of keys is precisely that window's distinct count. Taking the maximum checks all windows.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N) expected time with a hash map and O(K) memory. A zero frequency must stop contributing to the distinct count.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 3. ABC167_D -- Teleporter (approximately 800)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc167/tasks/abc167_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

A functional graph gives one next town for each town. Starting at town 1, report the town reached after exactly K moves, where K may be as large as 10^18.

## Recognition and derivation

Record the first step at which each visited town appears and store the walk order. The first repeated town identifies a tail and a cycle. If K passes the tail, reduce only the remaining distance modulo the cycle length.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Before the first repetition the walk has no choice and no duplicate. After entering the repeated suffix, determinism makes the same cycle repeat forever, so positions differing by its length are identical.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N) time and O(N) memory. K counts edges from the starting town at step 0; reduce K-tail, not K.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 4. ABC130_D -- Enough Array (approximately 900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc130/tasks/abc130_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

For a positive array, count subarrays whose sum is at least K. N is large enough that enumerating both endpoints is too slow.

## Recognition and derivation

For each left endpoint, advance a shared right endpoint until the window first reaches K. Positivity implies that every later right endpoint also works, contributing N-right choices, after which remove the left value.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Because all values are positive, extending a window cannot decrease its sum. Thus the first feasible right endpoint separates all infeasible endings from all feasible endings, and the pointer never needs to move backward.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary memory. Use a 64-bit answer; there can be N(N+1)/2 valid subarrays.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 5. ABC138_D -- Ki (approximately 900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc138/tasks/abc138_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

Root a tree at vertex 1. Each query adds a value to one vertex and every descendant of that vertex. Print the final value at every vertex.

## Recognition and derivation

Accumulate all query values directly at their named vertices. A single root-to-leaf traversal then adds the parent's accumulated value to each child.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

On reaching a vertex, its accumulator contains exactly the updates issued at its ancestors already propagated along the root path, plus its own updates. Passing that sum to children preserves the invariant.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N+Q) time and O(N) memory. The input edges are undirected; carry a parent or visited array.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 6. ABC218_E -- Destruction (approximately 1000)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc218/tasks/abc218_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

Delete edges from a connected weighted undirected graph while keeping it connected, maximizing the sum of deleted edge weights. Weights may be negative.

## Recognition and derivation

Keep every non-positive edge because deleting it cannot improve the score. Process positive edges by Kruskal order: keep one only when it joins different DSU components; otherwise delete it and add its weight.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Non-positive deletion is never beneficial. Among positive edges, the kept edges need only supply connectivity; Kruskal minimizes their total weight by the cut property, which equivalently maximizes the positive weight left for deletion.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(M log M) time and O(N) DSU memory. Blindly computing total minus an MST incorrectly deletes negative edges.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 7. ABC075_C -- Bridge (approximately 1100)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc075/tasks/abc075_c?lang=en>

## Restatement

In a small connected undirected graph, count edges whose individual removal disconnects the graph.

## Recognition and derivation

The small limits allow a direct definition-driven method: temporarily skip each edge, run DFS or BFS from one vertex, and test whether all vertices remain reachable.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

For a tested edge, reachability in the graph with exactly that edge removed is precisely the definition of whether it is a bridge. Testing every edge therefore counts all and only bridges.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(M(N+M)) time and O(N+M) memory. Skip an edge by its unique input index, not merely by its endpoints.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 8. ABC180_E -- Traveling Salesman among Aerial Cities (approximately 1300)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc180/tasks/abc180_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

Visit every 3D city, starting and ending at city 1. Travel cost is |dx|+|dy|+max(0,z_destination-z_source), so direction matters.

## Recognition and derivation

Use subset DP: dp[mask][v] is the minimum cost of starting at city 1, visiting exactly mask, and ending at v. Extend to each unvisited city, then add the directed cost back to city 1.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Every tour has a unique penultimate state obtained by deleting its last visited city. Conversely every transition appends one new city to a valid partial tour. Taking minima therefore covers exactly all visit orders.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N^2 2^N) time and O(N 2^N) memory. The height term makes cost(u,v) different from cost(v,u).

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 9. ABC137_D -- Summer Vacation (approximately 1300)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc137/tasks/abc137_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

There are M working days. Job i becomes available after A_i days and pays B_i; at most one job can be completed per day. Maximize reward.

## Recognition and derivation

Sort jobs by availability. Sweep the days, insert rewards of every job that has become available into a max-heap, and perform the currently most rewarding available job.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

On a day, replacing a chosen available job by the maximum-reward available job cannot reduce today's reward. The displaced lower-value job remains no less available for later days, so the exchange preserves feasibility.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O((N+M) log N) time and O(N) memory. Availability and deadlines are easy to reverse; trace the day convention.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 10. ABC135_D -- Digits Parade (approximately 1300)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc135/tasks/abc135_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

Replace every '?' in a decimal string by a digit. Count replacements whose resulting integer is congruent to 5 modulo 13, modulo 1e9+7.

## Recognition and derivation

Scan left to right. dp[r] counts assignments of the processed prefix with remainder r. Appending digit d changes r to (10r+d) mod 13; for '?' try all ten digits.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Each completed assignment has one previous-prefix remainder and one last digit, so it follows exactly one transition. Conversely every transition appends a permitted digit, making the DP a partition of all assignments by remainder.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(130|S|) time and O(13) memory. Reduce after every addition and distinguish the character '?' from a digit.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 11. ABC187_E -- Through Path (approximately 1400)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc187/tasks/abc187_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

Each query names a tree edge, chooses one of its two sides, and adds x to every vertex on that side. Print all final vertex values.

## Recognition and derivation

Root the tree. For a query affecting a child's subtree, add x at the child. For the complementary side, add x to a global/root difference and subtract x at that child. One prefix propagation resolves all queries.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

A rooted edge splits the tree into exactly the child's subtree and its complement. The two difference encodings mark precisely one of those sets; root-to-leaf prefix sums convert the markers into per-vertex totals.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N+Q) time and O(N) memory. Determine which endpoint is the child before interpreting the query type.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 12. ABC184_E -- Third Avenue (approximately 1400)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc184/tasks/abc184_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

Find a shortest path through a grid with walls. Equal lowercase letters are teleport stations: from a letter cell one move may reach any other cell with that letter.

## Recognition and derivation

Run BFS. When a letter is first expanded, enqueue every cell carrying that letter, then clear or mark that letter's list so it is never expanded globally again.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

BFS processes states in nondecreasing distance, so the first expansion of a letter already offers its cheapest possible teleport distance. Repeating the same complete teleport list later cannot improve any cell.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(HW) time and O(HW) memory. Without consuming each letter group once, repeated scans become quadratic.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 13. ABC245_F -- Endless Walk (approximately 1500)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc245/tasks/abc245_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

Count vertices of a directed graph from which one can follow directed edges forever.

## Recognition and derivation

Compress strongly connected components. A component is cyclic when it has at least two vertices or a self-loop. In the reversed condensation DAG, mark every component that can reach a cyclic component.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

An infinite walk in a finite graph must repeat a vertex and hence reach a directed cycle. Conversely, after reaching a cyclic SCC one can loop forever. Reverse reachability therefore characterizes exactly the valid starting components.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N+M) time and O(N+M) memory. A one-vertex SCC is cyclic only if it has a self-loop.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 14. ABC174_F -- Range Set Query (approximately 1500)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc174/tasks/abc174_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

Answer many inclusive array-range queries asking for the number of distinct colors.

## Recognition and derivation

Sort queries by right endpoint. During a left-to-right sweep, keep a Fenwick 1 only at the latest occurrence of each color: erase the old position, add the new one, then range-sum [L,R].

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

At sweep position R, a color contributes one marker to [L,R] exactly when its latest occurrence at or before R is at least L, which is equivalent to that color occurring in the queried range.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O((N+Q) log N) time and O(N+Q) memory. Queries must be answered only after the sweep reaches their R.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 15. ABC210_D -- National Railway (approximately 1500)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc210/tasks/abc210_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

Choose two distinct grid cells for stations. Their cost is both cell prices plus C times Manhattan distance; minimize it.

## Recognition and derivation

For a second station (i,j), the best earlier station contributes A[x][y]-C(x+y), while the new station contributes A[i][j]+C(i+j). Scan a direction while maintaining the minimum transformed value, then mirror columns and repeat for the missing orientation.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Within one scan orientation the Manhattan absolute values have fixed signs, so the pair cost separates into an earlier-station term and a current-station term. The mirrored pass covers every unordered pair.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(HW) time and O(1) extra memory beyond the grid. Update the answer before inserting the current cell to forbid choosing it twice.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 16. ABC190_E -- Magical Ornament (approximately 1600)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc190/tasks/abc190_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

In an unweighted graph, find the minimum number of visited vertices in a walk that visits every one of K special vertices, or report impossibility.

## Recognition and derivation

BFS from each special vertex to obtain pairwise shortest distances. Then run subset DP where dp[mask][last] is the minimum edge count of a walk visiting mask and ending at special vertex last.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Between consecutive special vertices an optimal walk may use a shortest path. The subset DP enumerates every order of first visits, and replacing each segment by its BFS distance cannot worsen a solution.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(K(N+M)+K^2 2^K) time and O(KN+K2^K) memory. The requested number of vertices is the minimum edge count plus one.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 17. ABC196_E -- Filters (approximately 1700)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc196/tasks/abc196_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

Compose many operations of three kinds on a number: add a, replace by max(x,a), or replace by min(x,a). Answer the final value for many inputs.

## Recognition and derivation

Any prefix of operations is a translated clamp: clamp(x+add, low, high). Update add and both bounds for an addition; update the bounds under max or min. Evaluate each query with the final triple.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

The identity is a translated clamp. Addition translates all three parameters, while max and min clamp both endpoints. Induction over the operations proves the representation remains exact.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N+Q) time and O(1) auxiliary memory. When a clamp crosses both bounds, both endpoints can collapse to one value.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 18. ABC204_E -- Rush Hour 2 (approximately 1700)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc204/tasks/abc204_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

An undirected edge entered at integer time t arrives at t+C+floor(D/(t+1)); waiting before entering is allowed. Find the earliest arrival from 1 to N.

## Recognition and derivation

Use Dijkstra, but relax an edge by minimizing f(t)=t+C+D/(t+1) over integer t at least the current time. The unconstrained minimum lies near sqrt(D), so test the current time and a small neighborhood around sqrt(D).

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

The discrete function decreases before its square-root region and increases after it; the constrained minimum is therefore either the current time or an integer next to sqrt(D). Exact relaxation costs are nonnegative and FIFO, so Dijkstra remains valid.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O((N+M) log N) time with a constant number of edge evaluations. Integer division and the t+1 denominator make off-by-one tests essential.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 19. ABC192_F -- Potion (approximately 1800)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc192/tasks/abc192_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

Choose a nonempty subset of the given positive values so that adding the same integer amount to every chosen value makes their sum equal X. Minimize that common added amount.

## Recognition and derivation

Fix subset size k. The chosen sum S must satisfy S congruent to X modulo k and S<=X; maximize such S with a DP over item count and remainder. The candidate answer is (X-S)/k. Try every k.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

For fixed k, a feasible common increment exists exactly under the two conditions above, and maximizing S minimizes the increment. The DP enumerates every k-element subset by its remainder, while the outer loop covers every possible subset size.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory under N<=100. Store the maximum sum for a state, not the minimum, and reject sums above X.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 20. ABC061_D -- Score Attack (approximately 1800)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc061/tasks/abc061_d?lang=en>

## Restatement

Find the maximum score of a directed path from vertex 1 to vertex N. If a positive cycle usable on such a path makes the score unbounded, print inf.

## Recognition and derivation

Negate edge scores and run Bellman-Ford minimization. Mark vertices whose distance can still improve on later rounds, propagate that mark forward, and report infinity only if N is marked and reachable.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

A post-(N-1)-round improvement is possible exactly through a reachable negative cycle in the negated graph. Propagation identifies vertices reachable after using such a cycle, so N is marked exactly when the original maximum can grow without bound.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(NM) time and O(N+M) memory. A positive cycle irrelevant to every 1-to-N path must not cause inf.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 21. ABC339_G -- Smaller Sum (approximately 1800)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc339/tasks/abc339_g?lang=en>

## Restatement

For online-decoded queries, return the sum of array values no greater than X inside [L,R]. Each query's parameters are XORed with the previous answer.

## Recognition and derivation

Build a merge-sort tree. At every node store its sorted values and their prefix sums. Decompose [L,R] into tree nodes; binary-search X in each node and add the corresponding prefix sum.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

The segment-tree decomposition partitions the query range. Within a node, upper_bound selects exactly values <=X, and its prefix sum counts each selected array element once. Online decoding happens before querying.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(log^2 N) per query and O(N log N) memory. Queries cannot be reordered because the previous answer decodes the next one.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 22. ABC172_E -- NEQ (approximately 1900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc172/tasks/abc172_e?lang=en>

## Restatement

Count ordered pairs of length-N injective sequences A and B over 1..M such that A_i differs from B_i at every position, modulo 1e9+7.

## Recognition and derivation

Choose A in P(M,N) ways. For a fixed A, apply inclusion-exclusion over positions forced to satisfy B_i=A_i: choosing k such positions leaves P(M-k,N-k) injective completions for B.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Each B with exactly t forbidden equalities appears in the alternating sum once for every subset of those t positions, with coefficient sum_k (-1)^k C(t,k), which is one when t=0 and zero otherwise.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N) time after O(M) factorial preprocessing and O(M) memory. The forced values also consume k distinct symbols from B's available pool.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 23. ABC285_F -- Substring of Sorted String (approximately 1900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc285/tasks/abc285_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

Support point character updates and queries asking whether a substring could appear as one contiguous block in the globally sorted string.

## Recognition and derivation

Maintain Fenwick counts for all 26 letters and another Fenwick marking descents S[i]>S[i+1]. A queried substring must have no descent. In addition, every globally present letter strictly between its endpoint letters must occur entirely inside the substring.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

A block of a sorted string is nondecreasing and cannot omit an occurrence of an intermediate letter, proving necessity. Those two conditions also place the substring's letter runs exactly where the corresponding global sorted runs occur, proving sufficiency.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(26 log N) per update or query and O(26N) memory. Only letters strictly between the first and last require full global counts.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 24. ABC223_F -- Parenthesis Checking (approximately 1900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc223/tasks/abc223_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

Support swaps of two parentheses and queries asking whether an inclusive substring is a correct bracket sequence.

## Recognition and derivation

Let pref[i] be the bracket balance through i. A substring [l,r] is valid when pref[r]=pref[l-1] and its minimum prefix on [l,r] is at least pref[l-1]. Swapping unequal endpoints is a range addition on the prefix array, handled by a lazy segment tree.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

The two conditions are exactly final balance zero and no relative prefix balance below zero. A swap changes contributions only between the two indices, so the stated range update keeps every pref value exact.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(log N) per operation and O(N) memory. The comparison baseline is pref[l-1], not zero in the global prefix array.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 25. ABC254_F -- Rectangle GCD (approximately 1900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc254/tasks/abc254_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

For arrays A and B, the conceptual matrix has value A_i+B_j. Answer the gcd of every value in many queried row-column rectangles.

## Recognition and derivation

Choose A_h1+B_w1 as a base. Every other value differs from it by a sum of adjacent differences from A and B. The rectangle gcd is the gcd of the base, gcd of A differences in its row interval, and gcd of B differences in its column interval.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

All matrix values are integer combinations of the three gcd inputs, so their gcd is a multiple of the computed value. Conversely each adjacent difference is a difference of two matrix cells, so the true rectangle gcd divides every input.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O((N+Q) log N) time with segment trees and O(N) memory. A one-row or one-column difference range is empty and contributes zero.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 26. ABC253_F -- Operations on a Matrix (approximately 1900)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc253/tasks/abc253_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

An initially zero matrix supports adding x to every cell in a column interval, assigning every cell of one row to x, and point-value queries.

## Recognition and derivation

Sweep operations offline with a Fenwick tree for column additions. For each point query, find the most recent assignment of its row. At that assignment time record and subtract the then-current column addition; at query time add the current one to the assigned base value.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

A row assignment erases exactly all column additions that occurred before it, while additions afterward remain effective. Subtracting the Fenwick value at the last assignment and adding its value at query time isolates precisely that suffix of additions.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O((N+Q) log M) time and O(N+Q) memory. Online storage of every matrix cell is impossible; bind queries to row assignments offline.

## Tests that matter

Test the smallest legal instance, every equality boundary mentioned
above, a case where the tempting literal algorithm chooses the wrong
state, and a maximum-shaped case that exercises the complexity bound.

# 27. ABC199_F -- Graph Smoothing (approximately 2100)

Official task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc199/tasks/abc199_f?lang=en>

## Restatement

Repeat a random edge-based averaging operation K times on graph vertex values and print the expected final value at every vertex modulo a prime.

## Recognition and derivation

Expectation is linear. Build an N by N transition matrix whose row describes one step's expected contribution to each vertex, including the probability that it is untouched. Raise the matrix to K and apply it to the initial-value vector.

Before implementing, write the slow literal model and identify exactly
which repeated work the stated representation removes.

## Correctness argument

Conditioning on the random edge and endpoint makes each next expected value a linear combination of current expected values. Thus one step is exactly matrix multiplication, and induction makes K steps T^K.

## Complexity and implementation traps

O(N^3 log K) time and O(N^2) memory. Convert division probabilities to modular inverses; do not simulate outcomes.

# Offline Companion Editorials

The entries below are full editorials for the original local companions.
Each companion includes complete C++ and Python references, a proof,
complexity analysis, and hostile-test guidance. It rehearses a nearby
course skill but is not the AtCoder task itself.

## 1. ABC083_B -- Some Sums: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc083/tasks/abc083_b?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/01_some_sums](problems/01_some_sums/README.md)

## Restatement

Given closed integer intervals with `l <= r`, print the largest number covering
one integer time and the smallest time with that coverage.

## Constraints and traps

The total interval count is `200000`, so scanning every integer coordinate is
impossible. Endpoints may be negative. Because intervals are closed, an
interval ending at x and one starting at x are both active at x; remove an
interval at `r+1`, not r.

## Closed-interval event model

For a closed integer interval `[l,r]`, add `+1` at l and `-1` at `r+1`.
After applying all changes at coordinate x, the running total is exactly the
number of intervals containing x. This `r+1` choice is the essential difference
from half-open events: intervals ending and starting at the same coordinate
are both active there.

For `[1,3]`, `[3,5]`, and `[3,3]`, events yield active counts one at 1, then
three at 3, so the answer is `3 3`.

```text
for each [l,r]: delta[l] += 1; delta[r+1] -= 1
active = 0; best = -1
for x in increasing event coordinates:
    active += delta[x]
    if active > best: best = active; answer_time = x
```

## Correctness and complexity

The prefix sum of delta at x equals every interval whose start is at most x
minus every interval whose end is before x, hence exactly the closed intervals
covering x. Counts only change at event coordinates, so the earliest coordinate
with a strict new maximum is the earliest busiest time. Sorted-map processing
costs `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` memory. Use `long long` coordinates in C++;
the local coordinate bound makes `r+1` safe. Test singleton intervals, touching
closed intervals, equal maximum counts at different times, and negative times.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int T;
    cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int n;
        cin >> n;

        map<long long, long long> delta;
        while (n--) {
            long long l, r;
            cin >> l >> r;
            ++delta[l];
            --delta[r + 1];
        }

        long long active = 0;
        long long best = -1;
        long long first_time = 0;
        for (auto [time, change] : delta) {
            active += change;
            if (active > best) {
                best = active;
                first_time = time;
            }
        }

        cout << best << ' ' << first_time << '\n';
    }
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return

    t = data[0]
    index = 1
    out: list[str] = []

    for _ in range(t):
        n = data[index]
        index += 1
        delta: dict[int, int] = {}

        for _ in range(n):
            l = data[index]
            r = data[index + 1]
            index += 2
            delta[l] = delta.get(l, 0) + 1
            delta[r + 1] = delta.get(r + 1, 0) - 1

        active = 0
        best = -1
        first_time = 0
        for time in sorted(delta):
            active += delta[time]
            if active > best:
                best = active
                first_time = time

        out.append(f"{best} {first_time}")

    sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## 2. ABC210_C -- Colorful Candies: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc210/tasks/abc210_c?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/02_colorful_candies](problems/02_colorful_candies/README.md)

## Restatement

Count the nonempty contiguous subarrays whose maximum value minus minimum value
is at most `k`. Array values may be negative; only the spread is constrained.

This is the section's blind-practice exercise. It needs two monotonic deques at
once: one to expose the current maximum and one to expose the current minimum.

## Observation and trace

For a fixed right endpoint, if `[left,right]` has acceptable spread, every
shorter suffix ending at `right` is also acceptable: removing values cannot
increase the maximum or decrease the minimum. Therefore after shrinking to a
valid window, all `right-left+1` starts from `left` through `right` contribute.

Keep decreasing values in the maximum deque and increasing values in the
minimum deque. Store indices, so expired positions can be removed when `left`
moves.

For `1 3 2 5` and `k=2`:

| right value | valid window after shrinking | new subarrays | answer |
|---:|:---|---:|---:|
| 1 | `[1]` | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | `[1,3]` | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | `[1,3,2]` | 3 | 6 |
| 5 | `[5]` | 1 | 7 |

At the last step the spread exceeds two until the left pointer has passed the
earlier values.

## Algorithm

```text
left = 0
max_deque = empty decreasing deque of indices
min_deque = empty increasing deque of indices
answer = 0

for right from 0 to n-1:
    remove dominated back indices from max_deque
    append right to max_deque
    remove dominated back indices from min_deque
    append right to min_deque

    while a[max_deque.front] - a[min_deque.front] > k:
        remove left from either deque when it is at the front
        left += 1

    answer += right-left+1
```

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After each update, the front of `max_deque` is an index of the
maximum value in the current window, and the front of `min_deque` is an index
of its minimum value.

**Proof.** When a new value arrives, every older maximum-deque back value no
larger than it is dominated: the new index lasts longer and is at least as
large. Removing those backs preserves all possible future maxima. The minimum
argument is symmetric for values no smaller than the new value. Expired front
indices are removed when the left endpoint passes them. Thus the surviving
fronts are exactly the needed extrema. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** After the shrinking loop, `[left,right]` has spread at most `k`,
and every subarray ending at `right` that starts before `left` is invalid.

**Proof.** Lemma 1 makes the loop condition exactly the current window's
spread. The loop stops only when it is at most `k`. Each discarded left index
belongs to a window whose spread was greater than `k`; extending that discarded
window farther left cannot reduce its spread, so any earlier start is invalid.
$\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm returns the required number of subarrays.

**Proof.** By Lemma 2, exactly the `right-left+1` suffixes ending at each
right endpoint are valid. The algorithm adds this number once per endpoint.
Every nonempty subarray has one right endpoint, so all and only valid subarrays
are counted once. $\square$

## Complexity

Each index enters and leaves each deque at most once. Time is `O(n)` per test
case and memory is `O(n)` in the worst case. The answer can be
`n(n+1)/2`, so use `long long` in C++.

## Implementation traps and tests

- Store indices, not just values, so you can remove expired endpoints.
- Use `<=` for the decreasing maximum deque and `>=` for the increasing
  minimum deque; retaining only the newest equal value is safe.
- Shrink before adding the count for the current right endpoint.
- Negative values are valid, so do not use a sum-based sliding window.

Test `k=0`, all equal values, alternating extreme values, a one-element array,
and the all-equal `200000`-element case that forces a 64-bit answer. The random
generator uses direct quadratic enumeration on small arrays.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int t;
    cin >> t;
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        long long k;
        cin >> n >> k;

        vector<long long> values(n);
        for (long long &value : values) cin >> value;

        deque<int> max_deque, min_deque;
        int left = 0;
        long long answer = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < n; ++right) {
            while (!max_deque.empty() &&
                   values[max_deque.back()] <= values[right]) {
                max_deque.pop_back();
            }
            max_deque.push_back(right);
            while (!min_deque.empty() &&
                   values[min_deque.back()] >= values[right]) {
                min_deque.pop_back();
            }
            min_deque.push_back(right);
            while (values[max_deque.front()] - values[min_deque.front()] > k) {
                if (max_deque.front() == left) {
                    max_deque.pop_front();
                }
                if (min_deque.front() == left) {
                    min_deque.pop_front();
                }
                ++left;
            }
            answer += right - left + 1;
        }
        cout << answer << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
from collections import deque
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    index = 1
    out: list[str] = []
    for _ in range(data[0]):
        n = data[index]
        k = data[index + 1]
        index += 2
        values = data[index:index + n]
        index += n

        max_deque: deque[int] = deque()
        min_deque: deque[int] = deque()
        left = 0
        answer = 0

        for right, value in enumerate(values):
            while max_deque and values[max_deque[-1]] <= value:
                max_deque.pop()
            max_deque.append(right)

            while min_deque and values[min_deque[-1]] >= value:
                min_deque.pop()
            min_deque.append(right)

            while values[max_deque[0]] - values[min_deque[0]] > k:
                if max_deque[0] == left:
                    max_deque.popleft()
                if min_deque[0] == left:
                    min_deque.popleft()
                left += 1

            answer += right - left + 1

        out.append(str(answer))

    sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# Stress testing

For next greater:

```text
For each i, scan j=i+1..n-1 and take the first greater value.
```

For sliding maximum:

```text
For each window, compute max directly.
```

For shortest subarray:

```text
Try every left endpoint and extend right while summing.
```

The local generators use these brute-force checks on small arrays.

# What to carry forward

The important habit is to identify dominance.

Ask:

- What makes an older candidate useless?
- Should equality remove the older candidate?
- Does the structure need values, indices, or both?
- When does a candidate expire?
- Can each candidate be pushed and popped only once?

These questions are the bridge from simple stacks and queues to later graph
BFS, DP optimization, and advanced monotonic data structures.

## 3. ABC167_D -- Teleporter: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc167/tasks/abc167_d?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/03_teleporter](problems/03_teleporter/README.md)

## Restatement

Every item has an activation level and a possibly negative weight. For each
query limit `x`, output the sum of weights of all items whose level is at most
`x`, preserving the input query order.

## Constraints and traps

Both `n` and `q` can be `200000`, so scanning all items for every query is
`O(nq)` and impossible. Query limits arrive in arbitrary order, and equal item
levels must all be included. Totals require `long long` in C++.

## Observation and walk-through

Sort items by level and queries as `(limit, original_id)`. Query limits then
only increase, so an item that has become active never needs removal.

For items `(5,10),(1,-3),(3,7),(5,2)`, the sorted sweep answers limits
`0,1,4,5` with `0,-3,4,16`. At limit `4`, exactly levels `1` and `3` have
entered the running sum. Store each answer by its original id before printing.

## Algorithm

```text
sort items by level
sort (query_limit, original_id) pairs by query_limit
sum = 0, item = 0
for (limit, id) in sorted queries:
    while item exists and items[item].level <= limit:
        sum += items[item].weight
        item += 1
    answer[id] = sum
print answers in id order
```

## Correctness proof

Before each sorted query limit `x`, the invariant is that `sum` contains
exactly the weights of items with level at most the previous processed limit.
The while-loop adds precisely the remaining items whose level is at most `x`;
because items are sorted, it adds no level above `x`. Thus `sum` is exactly the
required total for `x`. Saving it at the original id restores the answer to its
input position. Induction over sorted queries proves every printed total is
correct.

## Complexity

Sorting costs `O((n+q) log(n+q))`; the two pointers move forward at most `n+q`
times. Memory is `O(n+q)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n, q; cin >> n >> q;
    vector<pair<long long, long long>> items(n);
    for (auto &item : items) cin >> item.first >> item.second;
    vector<pair<long long, int>> queries(q);
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) cin >> queries[i].first, queries[i].second = i;
    sort(items.begin(), items.end());
    sort(queries.begin(), queries.end());
    vector<long long> answer(q);
    long long sum = 0;
    int item = 0;
    for (auto [limit, id] : queries) {
        while (item < n && items[item].first <= limit) sum += items[item++].second;
        answer[id] = sum;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) cout << answer[i] << " \n"[i + 1 == q];
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
n, q = data[0], data[1]
index = 2
items = sorted((data[i], data[i + 1]) for i in range(index, index + 2 * n, 2))
index += 2 * n
queries = sorted((data[index + i], i) for i in range(q))
answer = [0] * q
total = item = 0
for limit, query_id in queries:
    while item < n and items[item][0] <= limit:
        total += items[item][1]
        item += 1
    answer[query_id] = total
print(*answer)
```

## Tests that matter

Test queries below every level, duplicate levels, negative weights, and limits
that arrive in descending input order. The random oracle directly checks each
query against every small item; the scale case validates the offline sweep.

## 4. ABC130_D -- Enough Array: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc130/tasks/abc130_d?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/04_enough_array](problems/04_enough_array/README.md)

## Restatement

Given closed busy intervals within `0..limit` and a required integer duration
`d`, find the smallest start `s >= 0` whose entire interval
`[s, s+d-1]` is not busy. Return `-1` if no such start exists.

## Constraints and traps

The total number of intervals is at most `200000`, so testing every possible
start is impossible. Intervals are closed: if one ends at `r`, the earliest
time after it is `r+1`, not `r`. Input intervals may overlap, nest, or touch,
and `l <= r` is guaranteed. Use `long long` for `s+d-1`.

## Observation and walk-through

Sort closed busy intervals and maintain `cur`, the earliest time not already
blocked by processed intervals. If `cur+d-1 < l`, the gap before the next
interval fits and `cur` is the answer. Otherwise merge the obstacle by setting
`cur=max(cur,r+1)`. After all intervals, accept only when `cur+d-1<=limit`.

For busy intervals `[1,2],[5,7],[7,9]`, duration three, and limit twelve,
start `cur=0`. The initial candidate `[0,2]` overlaps `[1,2]`, so move to 3.
`[3,5]` overlaps `[5,7]`, so move to 8; `[8,10]` overlaps `[7,9]`, so move to
10. Finally `[10,12]` is free, so the answer is 10.

## Algorithm

```text
sort intervals by left endpoint
cur = 0
for [l, r] in sorted intervals:
    if cur + d - 1 < l: return cur
    cur = max(cur, r + 1)
return cur if cur + d - 1 <= limit else -1
```

## Correctness proof

The invariant is that no start below cur can still begin a legal slot after
the processed intervals. Sorting makes every future interval start no earlier
than the current one, so a fitting gap can be returned immediately. Each
interval either blocks the current candidate and advances `cur` past its right
endpoint, or leaves a gap large enough to return the smallest possible start.
After all intervals, the final limit test accepts exactly the remaining legal
candidate. Thus the algorithm returns the earliest valid start or `-1`.

## Complexity

Sorting costs `O(n log n)`, the scan is linear, and memory is `O(n)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int tests; cin >> tests;
    while (tests--) {
        int n; long long duration, limit;
        cin >> n >> duration >> limit;
        vector<pair<long long, long long>> busy(n);
        for (auto &interval : busy) cin >> interval.first >> interval.second;
        sort(busy.begin(), busy.end());
        long long cur = 0;
        for (auto [left, right] : busy) {
            if (cur + duration - 1 < left) break;
            cur = max(cur, right + 1);
        }
        cout << (cur + duration - 1 <= limit ? cur : -1) << '\n';
    }
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys

data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
index = 1
out = []
for _ in range(data[0]):
    n, duration, limit = data[index:index + 3]
    index += 3
    busy = sorted((data[i], data[i + 1]) for i in range(index, index + 2 * n, 2))
    index += 2 * n
    cur = 0
    for left, right in busy:
        if cur + duration - 1 < left:
            break
        cur = max(cur, right + 1)
    out.append(str(cur if cur + duration - 1 <= limit else -1))
print("\n".join(out))
```

## Tests that matter

Test no intervals, touching intervals such as `[2,2]` and `[3,3]`, nested
intervals, and a valid slot ending exactly at `limit`. The small oracle scans
integer starts; the scale case checks the sorted scan is necessary.

## 5. ABC138_D -- Ki: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc138/tasks/abc138_d?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/05_ki](problems/05_ki/README.md)

## Restatement

An undirected, unweighted graph contains several station vertices.  For every
vertex, print the minimum number of edges needed to reach any station.  Print
`-1` when its connected component contains no station.

The graph can have up to `200000` vertices and edges, so running an ordinary
BFS separately from every vertex, or separately from every station, can be
too slow.

## Key idea: start BFS from every station

Imagine adding one virtual source connected to every station by a zero-length
edge.  The desired answer is the shortest distance from that virtual source.
We do not need to build the virtual source: put every station in the BFS queue
initially and assign all of them distance `0`.

Then run the usual BFS.  When a vertex `v` is first discovered from `u`, write

```text
dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
```

Vertices in components without stations are never put in the queue, so their
initial value `-1` remains the correct answer.

## Walk-through

For the chain below, stations are vertices `1` and `5`:

```text
1 -- 2 -- 3 -- 4 -- 5
```

Initial queue and distances:

```text
queue: [1, 5]
dist:  [0, -1, -1, -1, 0]
```

Processing `1` discovers `2`; processing `5` discovers `4`.  Both receive
distance `1`.  Next, either `2` or `4` discovers `3`, which receives distance
`2`.  The answer is therefore:

```text
0 1 2 1 0
```

It does not matter which same-distance vertex is popped first.  BFS always
processes all vertices at distance `d` before any vertex at distance `d + 1`.

## Algorithm

```text
build an adjacency list for the undirected graph
set every dist value to -1

for every station s:
    if dist[s] is -1:          # harmless if a station is listed twice
        dist[s] = 0
        push s into the queue

while the queue is not empty:
    u = pop from the front
    for every neighbor v of u:
        if dist[v] is -1:
            dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
            push v into the queue

print dist[1], dist[2], ..., dist[n]
```

## Correctness proof

We prove that the algorithm prints the required distance for every vertex.

Every station is inserted with distance `0`, so its printed value is correct.
Consider a non-station vertex `v` that is first discovered from `u`.  BFS
processes vertices in nondecreasing distance order.  Thus `u` has the minimum
possible distance to any station among vertices that could first reach `v`.
Appending edge `(u, v)` gives a path of length `dist[u] + 1` from a station to
`v`, so the algorithm assigns a reachable distance to `v`.

Suppose a shorter station-to-`v` path of length `L` existed.  Let `w` be the
vertex directly before `v` on that path.  Because
`L < dist[v] = dist[u] + 1`, we have `L - 1 < dist[u]`.  BFS reaches and
processes `w` before `u`, then discovers `v` with a value at most `L`.  This
contradicts the assignment of the larger value `dist[u] + 1`.  Therefore
`dist[v]` is the minimum distance to any station.

Finally, an unvisited vertex cannot be connected to a station: a path from a
station would make BFS traverse its edges and discover it.  Its value remains
`-1`, which is correct.  Hence all printed values are correct.

## Complexity

Each vertex enters the queue at most once and each undirected edge is examined
twice.  The time complexity is `O(n + m)` and the adjacency list, distances,
and queue use `O(n + m)` memory.

## Reference implementation in C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m, k;
    cin >> n >> m >> k;

    vector<vector<int>> graph(n + 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        cin >> u >> v;
        graph[u].push_back(v);
        graph[v].push_back(u);
    }

    vector<int> dist(n + 1, -1);
    queue<int> q;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
        int station;
        cin >> station;
        if (dist[station] == -1) {
            dist[station] = 0;
            q.push(station);
        }
    }

    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        for (int v : graph[u]) {
            if (dist[v] == -1) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                q.push(v);
            }
        }
    }

    for (int v = 1; v <= n; ++v) {
        cout << dist[v] << (v == n ? '\\n' : ' ');
    }
}
```

## Reference implementation in Python

```python
import sys
from collections import deque


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    n, m, k = data[:3]
    index = 3

    graph = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for _ in range(m):
        u, v = data[index], data[index + 1]
        index += 2
        graph[u].append(v)
        graph[v].append(u)

    dist = [-1] * (n + 1)
    q = deque()
    for station in data[index:index + k]:
        if dist[station] == -1:
            dist[station] = 0
            q.append(station)

    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for v in graph[u]:
            if dist[v] == -1:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                q.append(v)

    print(*dist[1:])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Tests worth checking

- One station in a disconnected component: vertices in other components must
  remain `-1`.
- Stations at both ends of a path: the middle vertex uses the closer end.
- Adjacent stations and duplicated station input: every station still has
  distance `0`.
- A long chain with one station at an endpoint: checks both linear time and
  queue behavior.

## 6. ABC218_E -- Destruction: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc218/tasks/abc218_e?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/06_destruction](problems/06_destruction/README.md)

## Restatement

The input is an undirected simple graph that can be disconnected. Classify
every connected component as either a tree component (it has no cycle) or a
cyclic component (it has at least one cycle), then print the two counts.

## Constraints and traps

Both the number of vertices and roads can be `200000`, so repeatedly scanning
the graph for every component, or doing a separate cycle search after every
traversal, risks unnecessary work. Isolated vertices count: a one-vertex,
zero-edge component is a tree. Every undirected road appears in two adjacency
lists, so summing degrees counts each road twice.

The graph is simple: there are no self-loops or repeated roads. That makes the
standard connected-component characterization especially clean:

```text
connected component is a tree  <=>  number of edges = number of vertices - 1
```

## Observation and walk-through

Run one iterative DFS from each unvisited vertex. During that traversal,
increment `vertices` whenever a vertex is popped, and add the length of its
adjacency list to `degree_sum`. At the end, the component has
`edges = degree_sum / 2` roads.

For the sample, DFS from `1` sees vertices `1, 2, 3`. Its degree sum is
`1 + 2 + 1 = 4`, so it has two edges and is a tree because `2 = 3 - 1`.
DFS from `4` sees a triangle: three vertices and degree sum `6`, hence three
edges. Since `3 != 3 - 1`, that component is cyclic. Finally, `7--8` is a
second tree component.

## Algorithm

```text
build an undirected adjacency list
seen[v] = false for every vertex
tree_components = cyclic_components = 0

for every vertex start:
    if start is seen:
        continue

    vertices = degree_sum = 0
    mark start and push it onto a stack
    while stack is not empty:
        u = pop stack
        vertices += 1
        degree_sum += number of neighbors of u
        for every neighbor v of u:
            if v is unseen:
                mark v
                push v

    edges = degree_sum / 2
    if edges == vertices - 1:
        tree_components += 1
    else:
        cyclic_components += 1

print tree_components and cyclic_components
```

Mark a vertex when it is pushed, not when it is popped. Otherwise two
neighbors can push the same vertex before either copy is processed.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** One DFS started at an unvisited vertex visits exactly its connected
component, and no other component.

**Proof.** Every visited vertex is reached through a chain of graph edges from
the start, so it belongs to the start's component. Conversely, DFS follows
every edge incident to every vertex it visits. Any vertex connected to the
start has a path from it; proceeding along that path shows DFS eventually
marks every vertex on the path, including the endpoint. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** After one DFS, `vertices` and `degree_sum / 2` are respectively
the number of vertices and edges in that connected component.

**Proof.** By Lemma 1, each component vertex is popped exactly once and adds
one to `vertices`. Every component road appears once in the adjacency list of
each endpoint, so it contributes exactly two to `degree_sum`. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** A connected component is a tree exactly when its edge count is
one less than its vertex count.

**Proof.** A tree with `V` vertices has `V-1` edges: start with one vertex and
each newly attached vertex contributes one edge. Conversely, a connected graph
with `V-1` edges cannot contain a cycle. Removing an edge from a cycle keeps
the graph connected, which would leave a connected graph with only `V-2`
edges; a connected graph needs at least `V-1` edges to reach all `V` vertices.
Thus it is acyclic and therefore a tree. $\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the correct number of tree and cyclic
components.

**Proof.** The outer loop starts exactly one DFS for each connected component.
By Lemma 2 it computes that component's exact vertex and edge counts, and by
Lemma 3 it classifies the component correctly. Adding one to the matching
counter for every component gives exactly both requested totals. $\square$

## Complexity

Every vertex is pushed once and every undirected road is scanned from each of
its two endpoints.

```text
Time:   O(n + m)
Memory: O(n + m)
```

## C++ implementation notes

Store `degree_sum` in `long long`. It fits in `int` under these bounds, but the
type makes the relationship to an edge count explicit and remains safe if the
exercise limits later grow. A `vector<char>` is enough for the `seen` state.

## Python implementation notes

Use a normal list as a stack with `append` and `pop`; both are amortized
constant time. Read all integers from `sys.stdin.buffer` to avoid repeated
input overhead on the scale case.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;
    vector<vector<int>> graph(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        cin >> u >> v;
        --u;
        --v;
        graph[u].push_back(v);
        graph[v].push_back(u);
    }

    vector<char> seen(n, false);
    int tree_components = 0, cyclic_components = 0;
    for (int start = 0; start < n; ++start) {
        if (seen[start]) continue;

        long long vertices = 0, degree_sum = 0;
        vector<int> stack = {start};
        seen[start] = true;
        while (!stack.empty()) {
            int u = stack.back();
            stack.pop_back();
            ++vertices;
            degree_sum += graph[u].size();
            for (int v : graph[u]) {
                if (!seen[v]) {
                    seen[v] = true;
                    stack.push_back(v);
                }
            }
        }

        if (degree_sum / 2 == vertices - 1) ++tree_components;
        else ++cyclic_components;
    }

    cout << tree_components << ' ' << cyclic_components << '\n';
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    n, m = data[0], data[1]
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    index = 2
    for _ in range(m):
        u = data[index] - 1
        v = data[index + 1] - 1
        index += 2
        graph[u].append(v)
        graph[v].append(u)

    seen = [False] * n
    tree_components = cyclic_components = 0
    for start in range(n):
        if seen[start]:
            continue

        vertices = degree_sum = 0
        stack = [start]
        seen[start] = True
        while stack:
            u = stack.pop()
            vertices += 1
            degree_sum += len(graph[u])
            for v in graph[u]:
                if not seen[v]:
                    seen[v] = True
                    stack.append(v)

        if degree_sum // 2 == vertices - 1:
            tree_components += 1
        else:
            cyclic_components += 1

    print(tree_components, cyclic_components)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Common wrong answers

- Starting DFS only from vertex `1`, which ignores other components.
- Calling every component with at least one edge cyclic; a path has edges but
  is still a tree.
- Comparing `degree_sum` directly with `vertices - 1` instead of dividing by
  two.
- Marking vertices only on pop, allowing duplicate stack entries and corrupting
  the collected statistics.

## Tests that matter

- no roads: every isolated vertex is a tree component;
- one triangle plus a path: checks both categories in one graph;
- a cycle with a long tail: it remains one cyclic component;
- nested-looking traversal order with many cross edges: edge counting must not
  depend on DFS parent choices;
- a `200000`-vertex cycle: rejects recursive implementations that exhaust the
  call stack and quadratic repeated traversals.

# Stress testing

Good stress tests for this section compare independent ideas:

Problem A:

```text
generate a random tree
compute subtree sizes with the iterative method
compare with a slow recursive method on small n
```

Problem B:

```text
for each connected component, count vertices and edges
in a simple undirected graph, a connected component is cyclic iff edges >= vertices
```

Problem C:

```text
compare DFS colors against Floyd-Warshall reachability on tiny directed graphs:
there is a cycle iff some edge u->v has v reachable back to u
```

Problem D:

```text
brute-force every connected component with a tiny BFS
count its vertices and unique undirected edges
classify it using edges == vertices - 1
```

The local generators use direct reference implementations and include both
fixed edge cases and randomized cases for C++ and Python.

# What to carry forward

DFS is the tool to reach for when:

```text
the graph is unweighted but shortest distance is not the point
the problem asks about descendants or subtrees
you need to know when a branch is finished
you need to detect cycles
```

The next section builds on DFS finishing order and introduces topological
sorting and dynamic programming on DAGs.

## 7. ABC075_C -- Bridge: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc075/tasks/abc075_c?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/07_bridge](problems/07_bridge/README.md)

## Restatement

Each directed edge `a -> b` says that build step `a` must occur before step
`b`.  There are three possible outcomes:

- a directed cycle makes every complete build order impossible;
- an acyclic graph can have two or more valid orders, so the answer is
  `AMBIGUOUS`;
- otherwise there is exactly one valid order, which must be printed.

The graph has up to `200000` vertices and edges.  Trying permutations is useful
only for a tiny brute-force tester, not for the submitted solution.

## Observation: available choices determine uniqueness

Run Kahn's algorithm and consider the set of currently available vertices:
those with indegree `0` after already chosen vertices have been removed.

- If it is empty before all vertices are processed, a cycle remains.
- If it ever contains two or more vertices, either one may be chosen next.
  Those two choices begin two distinct valid topological orders.
- If it contains exactly one vertex at every step and all vertices are
  processed, every position is forced.  The order is unique.

The queue does not need to be a min-heap.  When the order is unique there is
only one possible next vertex; when it is ambiguous we print no order.  A
plain FIFO queue is therefore sufficient.

Do not immediately print `AMBIGUOUS` after seeing two available vertices.  A
separate component may still contain a cycle.  Continue Kahn's algorithm and
let `IMPOSSIBLE` take priority if fewer than `n` vertices are processed.

## Walk-through

First consider a forced chain:

```text
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4
```

The available set has one member at every stage:

```text
available: {1} -> {2} -> {3} -> {4}
order:       1      2      3      4
```

So the result is:

```text
UNIQUE
1 2 3 4
```

Now add two independent starting steps:

```text
1 -> 3 <- 2
```

Initially both `1` and `2` have indegree `0`:

```text
available: {1, 2}
```

Choosing `1` first gives `1, 2, 3`; choosing `2` first gives `2, 1, 3`.
Thus the graph is `AMBIGUOUS`.

Finally, a graph can look ambiguous locally and still be impossible overall:

```text
1 -> 3 <- 2       4 <-> 5
```

Steps `1` and `2` are initially available, but `4` and `5` can never be
removed.  The correct answer is `IMPOSSIBLE`, not `AMBIGUOUS`.

## Algorithm

```text
build adjacency lists and indegree values
put every vertex with indegree 0 into a queue
ambiguous = false
order = empty list

while queue is not empty:
    if queue has at least two vertices:
        ambiguous = true

    remove one vertex u from the queue
    append u to order
    for every edge u -> v:
        decrease indegree[v]
        if indegree[v] becomes 0:
            add v to the queue

if order has fewer than n vertices:
    print IMPOSSIBLE
else if ambiguous:
    print AMBIGUOUS
else:
    print UNIQUE and order
```

## Correctness proof

We prove that the algorithm prints the required classification and, when
applicable, the required order.

**Lemma 1.** If the algorithm processes fewer than `n` vertices, the graph
contains a directed cycle.

**Proof.** Kahn's algorithm stops only when no unprocessed vertex has
indegree `0` within the remaining graph.  Starting from any remaining vertex
and repeatedly following an incoming remaining edge must eventually repeat a
vertex because the remaining graph is finite.  The repeated portion is a
directed cycle. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** If at some iteration the queue contains two different vertices,
the graph has at least two valid topological orders.

**Proof.** Both vertices have no unprocessed prerequisites, so either can be
placed next after the already constructed prefix.  Removing either available
vertex from a DAG leaves a DAG, which Kahn's algorithm can complete.  One
completion starts with the first chosen vertex and another starts with the
second, so the two valid orders differ at this position. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** If the algorithm processes all vertices and the queue has exactly
one vertex at every iteration, the recorded order is the only valid
topological order.

**Proof.** Induct on the position in the order.  Before the first position,
the only indegree-zero vertex is the only vertex that can legally be first.
After that forced vertex is removed, the same argument applies to the unique
available vertex for the next position.  Every position is forced, so no
different valid order exists. $\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the correct output.

**Proof.** By Lemma 1, fewer than `n` processed vertices means `IMPOSSIBLE` is
correct.  Otherwise the graph is acyclic.  If `ambiguous` is true, Lemma 2
gives two valid orders, so `AMBIGUOUS` is correct.  If it is false, Lemma 3
proves that the recorded topological order is unique, so printing `UNIQUE`
and that order is correct. $\square$

## Complexity

Every vertex enters the queue once, and every edge is examined once:

```text
Time:   O(n + m)
Memory: O(n + m)
```

## Implementation notes

- Check `queue.size()` or `len(queue)` before removing the next vertex.
- Keep processing after finding multiple available vertices; a cycle has
  higher-priority output.
- Record the order only so it can be printed in the unique case.
- With `n, m <= 200000`, use adjacency lists and an iterative queue.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;

    vector<vector<int>> graph(n + 1);
    vector<int> indegree(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int a, b;
        cin >> a >> b;
        graph[a].push_back(b);
        ++indegree[b];
    }

    queue<int> available;
    for (int step = 1; step <= n; ++step) {
        if (indegree[step] == 0) {
            available.push(step);
        }
    }

    bool ambiguous = false;
    vector<int> order;
    while (!available.empty()) {
        if (available.size() > 1) {
            ambiguous = true;
        }

        int u = available.front();
        available.pop();
        order.push_back(u);
        for (int v : graph[u]) {
            --indegree[v];
            if (indegree[v] == 0) {
                available.push(v);
            }
        }
    }

    if (static_cast<int>(order.size()) != n) {
        cout << "IMPOSSIBLE\\n";
    } else if (ambiguous) {
        cout << "AMBIGUOUS\\n";
    } else {
        cout << "UNIQUE\\n";
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            cout << order[i] << (i + 1 == n ? '\\n' : ' ');
        }
    }
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
from collections import deque


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    n, m = data[:2]
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    indegree = [0] * (n + 1)
    index = 2
    for _ in range(m):
        a, b = data[index], data[index + 1]
        index += 2
        graph[a].append(b)
        indegree[b] += 1

    available = deque(step for step in range(1, n + 1) if indegree[step] == 0)
    ambiguous = False
    order = []
    while available:
        if len(available) > 1:
            ambiguous = True

        u = available.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                available.append(v)

    if len(order) != n:
        print("IMPOSSIBLE")
    elif ambiguous:
        print("AMBIGUOUS")
    else:
        print("UNIQUE")
        print(*order)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Common wrong answers

- Printing `AMBIGUOUS` as soon as two vertices are available, then missing a
  cycle in another component.
- Checking only the initial indegree-zero set.  Choices can appear later.
- Using a min-heap because a previous task requested lexicographic order.
  This problem asks about uniqueness, not the smallest order.
- Treating a vertex with outgoing edges as unavailable.  Only unmet incoming
  dependencies affect availability.

## Tests that matter

- a one-vertex graph, which is uniquely ordered;
- a long chain, which is uniquely ordered;
- no edges on several vertices, which is ambiguous immediately;
- two independent starting vertices that later merge;
- a cycle with no initial available vertex;
- two available vertices plus a separate directed cycle, which must print
  `IMPOSSIBLE`.

# Stress testing

For Problem D, keep random graphs very small and enumerate permutations of all
vertices.  Count valid orders only until the second one:

```text
zero valid permutations -> IMPOSSIBLE
one valid permutation  -> UNIQUE and that permutation
two valid permutations -> AMBIGUOUS
```

This oracle is deliberately different from the submitted Kahn-based solution.
It catches mistakes such as declaring ambiguity before ruling out a cycle.  A
separate large acyclic graph with two initial sources checks that the actual
solution remains linear at `200000` vertices and edges.

# What to carry forward

Topological sorting is more than a way to produce an order.  The set of
currently available vertices records what dependency choices remain:

```text
no available vertex before completion -> cycle
one available vertex at every step     -> forced order
two available vertices at some step    -> at least two orders
```

Whenever a directed dependency graph is acyclic, process it in a topological
order and ask what state can be propagated along each forward edge.

## 8. ABC180_E -- Traveling Salesman among Aerial Cities: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc180/tasks/abc180_e?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/08_traveling_salesman_among_aerial_cities](problems/08_traveling_salesman_among_aerial_cities/README.md)

## Restatement

We may deactivate cables in an undirected weighted graph.  The remaining
network must preserve the original connectivity relation: if two computers
were connected by some path before deactivation, they must still have a path
afterwards.  Different original connected components do not need to become
connected.

We want the greatest total cost of deactivated cables.  Cable costs are
nonnegative, and `n, m` can both reach `200000`, so checking connectivity after
each possible removal is far too slow.

## Observation: keep a minimum spanning forest

Let `total` be the sum of all cable costs.  Maximizing removed cost is the same
as minimizing the cost of the cables we keep:

```text
saved cost = total - kept cost
```

Consider one original connected component.  The kept cables only need to keep
that component connected.  A minimum-cost connected subgraph can be reduced to
a tree: if it contains a cycle, removing any edge on that cycle keeps it
connected and never increases cost because all costs are nonnegative.  Thus we
need a minimum spanning tree for each original component.

Together, those trees form a **minimum spanning forest**.  Kruskal's algorithm
already builds exactly that forest if we simply process every edge and never
declare a disconnected graph impossible.

## Walk-through

Suppose the graph has two original components:

```text
component 1:  1 --4-- 2 --1-- 3
                 \       /
                  ---3---

component 2:  4 --7-- 5
```

Process edges in increasing cost:

```text
2-3, cost 1: keep
1-3, cost 3: keep
1-2, cost 4: skip; it would make a cycle
4-5, cost 7: keep
```

The kept forest costs `1 + 3 + 7 = 11`.  All cable costs total `15`, so the
maximum saving is:

```text
15 - 11 = 4
```

An isolated vertex needs no kept cable and contributes neither kept cost nor
saved cost.

## Algorithm

```text
read all edges and add their weights to total
sort edges by increasing weight
make a DSU with one component per vertex
kept = 0

for every edge (u, v, w) in sorted order:
    if union(u, v) succeeds:
        kept += w

print total - kept
```

Unlike a connected-MST problem, do not check whether exactly `n - 1` edges
were kept.  A disconnected input is valid: Kruskal returns one tree for each
component.

## Correctness proof

We prove that the algorithm outputs the maximum possible saved cost.

**Lemma 1.** In every original connected component, there is an optimal set of
