## 41. AGC006_D -- Median Pyramid Hard: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc006/tasks/agc006_d?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/41_median_pyramid_hard](problems/41_median_pyramid_hard/README.md)

## Restatement and first invariant

Two binary strings `A` and `B` have equal length `n`. One operation chooses an
adjacent pair and flips both bits. Find the minimum number of operations needed
to turn `A` into `B`, or `-1` if it is impossible. Here `n` can be 200,000, so
searching over strings is not viable.

Every operation changes exactly two bits, so the parity of the number of ones
is invariant. Equivalently, the XOR of all bits is invariant. This gives a
necessary condition, but it does not yet identify a shortest construction. The
path shape of the allowed pairs gives a stronger left-to-right recurrence.

## Forced recurrence and trace

Let `d[i] = A[i] xor B[i]`; it says whether position `i` must be flipped an
odd number of times. After cancelling pairs of identical operations, use each
edge operation zero or one time. Let `x[i]` denote whether the operation
flipping positions `i` and `i+1` is used.

Position 1 is touched only by `x[1]`, so `x[1] = d[1]`. For every interior
position, the two touching operations must satisfy:

```text
x[i-1] xor x[i] = d[i]
x[i] = d[i] xor x[i-1]
```

For `A=0000` and `B=1001`, the mismatch vector is `1,0,0,1`:

```text
x[1] = 1
x[2] = 0 xor 1 = 1
x[3] = 0 xor 1 = 1
```

The final position is touched only by `x[3]`; it needs `d[4]=1`, so this
construction works and uses three operations. If the final check disagrees,
no choice remains to repair it.

## Algorithm

```text
previous_operation = 0
answer = 0
for i from 1 to n-1:
    mismatch = A[i] xor B[i]
    current_operation = mismatch xor previous_operation
    answer += current_operation
    previous_operation = current_operation

if previous_operation != (A[n] xor B[n]):
    print -1
else:
    print answer
```

For `n=1`, the loop is empty and the final check correctly says that only
identical strings are reachable.

## Correctness proof

Cancelling two uses of the same adjacent operation changes no bit, so an
optimal sequence uses each operation at most once. In such a sequence,
position 1 forces `x[1]=d[1]`. Assuming `x[i-1]` is forced, position `i` is
correct exactly when `x[i-1] xor x[i]=d[i]`, which forces the stated value of
`x[i]`. By induction, the algorithm produces the only possible reduced choice
for all operations through `x[n-1]`.

The final position is touched only by `x[n-1]`. If its value differs from
`d[n]`, no reduced sequence can reach `B`, so `-1` is correct. Otherwise every
position satisfies its mismatch equation, so applying exactly the selected
operations transforms `A` into `B`. Any sequence has the same forced parity
for each operation; after cancellation it has exactly this selected set, so no
sequence can use fewer operations. The reported count is therefore minimal.
QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

The scan is `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra space. Treat `0` and `1` characters as
bits; no integer conversion of the entire strings is necessary. Test `n=1`,
an odd mismatch count, endpoint-only mismatches, and a target produced by
flipping alternating adjacent pairs. A common mistake is to check only the
global XOR invariant and assume that it also constructs the minimum.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n;
    string start, target;
    if (!(cin >> n >> start >> target)) return 0;

    int previous_operation = 0;
    int answer = 0;
    for (int index = 0; index + 1 < n; index++) {
        int mismatch = start[index] != target[index];
        int current_operation = mismatch ^ previous_operation;
        answer += current_operation;
        previous_operation = current_operation;
    }

    if (previous_operation != (start[n - 1] != target[n - 1])) cout << -1 << '\n';
    else cout << answer << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    n = int(data[0])
    start = data[1]
    target = data[2]

    previous_operation = 0
    answer = 0
    for index in range(n - 1):
        mismatch = start[index] != target[index]
        current_operation = int(mismatch) ^ previous_operation
        answer += current_operation
        previous_operation = current_operation

    if previous_operation != (start[-1] != target[-1]):
        print(-1)
    else:
        print(answer)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# What to carry forward

# Complete upsolve notes

## A. Same Parity
An operation changes a value by two, so parity is invariant. Mixed parity makes
equality impossible. If all residues match, move every value by repeated +/-2
steps to a common value, proving sufficiency. Scan residues once: `O(n)` time,
`O(1)` memory. Test one value, all even, all odd, and one mixed pair.

## B. XOR Balanced Splits
Let total XOR be T and a prefix XOR be P. The suffix is `T xor P`, so equality
is equivalent to T=0. Thus answer is n-1 when total XOR is zero, otherwise
zero. This is O(n); test n=1 and zero/nonzero totals. Do not recompute suffix
XOR for every cut.

## C. Same Residue
Adding or subtracting k preserves residue modulo k. Equal residues are also
sufficient because values differ by multiples of k. Compare every `a[i] % k`
to the first; normalize negatives in a generalized C++ version. O(n) time,
O(1) memory; test k=1 and a mixed-residue pair.

Use `long long` for values in C++ and direct integers in Python. Run the local
suite and brute-force very small states to test the claimed reachability class.

Red-level improvement comes from making the invariant explicit, stress-testing it, and then upsolving the stronger external versions.

For D, tiny tests use BFS over all `2^n` binary strings to obtain the true
shortest distance, not a copy of the recurrence. The scale case uses 200,000
bits and a directly known all-edge operation pattern.

## 42. ARC108_E -- Random IS: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc108/tasks/arc108_e?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/42_random_is](problems/42_random_is/README.md)

## Restatement and traps

There are several piles, and one turn changes exactly one pile by subtracting
an allowed amount. The game ends only when every pile has no legal subtraction.
This is not a single subtraction game with the pile sizes added together: a
move in one pile does not alter the legal moves in another pile.

The largest pile size is at most `200000` and there are at most twenty move
sizes. Simulating play on all combinations of pile sizes is impossible, but one
pile has only `maximum_pile + 1` states.

## One-pile Grundy values

Let `g[x]` be the Grundy value of one pile containing `x` stones. Its moves go
to the states `x-d` for allowed `d <= x`, so the defining recurrence is

```text
g[0] = 0
g[x] = mex({ g[x-d] : d is allowed and d <= x })
```

Compute these values from zero through the largest input pile. At most `m`
values are reachable from a state, so the mex is at most `m`; a small boolean
array or set is enough.

For moves `{1,3,4}`, the first values are:

```text
x       0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
g[x]    0 1 0 1 2 3 2 0
```

## Combining piles and trace

The piles are independent impartial games. Their combined Grundy value is the
xor of their individual values. The initial position is losing exactly when
that xor is zero.

In the sample, the table gives `g[2]=0`, `g[4]=2`, and `g[7]=0`. The total is
`0 xor 2 xor 0 = 2`, so the first player has a winning move and the answer is
`WIN`.

## Algorithm

```text
read every pile and let H be the largest size
for x from 1 through H:
    g[x] = mex of g[x-d] over legal allowed moves d
xor g[pile] for every input pile
print WIN iff the xor is nonzero
```

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** For every pile size `x`, the computed value `g[x]` is its Grundy
number in the one-pile subtraction game.

**Proof.** `g[0]=0` because no move is possible. Every move from `x` reaches a
smaller pile `x-d`, whose Grundy number has already been computed correctly.
Taking the mex of exactly those reachable values is the definition of the
Grundy number. Induction on `x` proves the lemma.

**Lemma 2.** The xor of the computed Grundy values is the Grundy value of the
whole multi-pile position.

**Proof.** A turn chooses one pile and leaves all other piles unchanged, so the
position is the disjoint sum of its one-pile games. The Sprague-Grundy xor rule
states that the Grundy value of such a sum is the xor of the component values.

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints `WIN` exactly when the first player can force
a win.

**Proof.** By Lemma 1 the values used for every pile are correct, and by Lemma
2 their xor is the combined Grundy value. An impartial normal-play position is
losing exactly when its Grundy value is zero, so the reported condition is
exactly the winning condition.

## Complexity and implementation notes

Let `H` be the largest input pile and `m` the number of moves. The DP takes
`O(H*m)` time, and reading/xoring piles takes `O(p)`. Memory is `O(H)`. Do not
compute only winning/losing values: xor needs the full Grundy numbers. Zero-size
piles contribute `g[0]=0` and therefore change nothing.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int move_count, pile_count;
    if (!(cin >> move_count >> pile_count)) return 0;
    vector<int> moves(move_count), piles(pile_count);
    for (int& move : moves) cin >> move;
    int maximum = 0;
    for (int& pile : piles) {
        cin >> pile;
        maximum = max(maximum, pile);
    }

    vector<int> grundy(maximum + 1);
    for (int stones = 1; stones <= maximum; ++stones) {
        bool seen[32]{};
        for (int move : moves) {
            if (move <= stones) seen[grundy[stones - move]] = true;
        }
        while (seen[grundy[stones]]) ++grundy[stones];
    }
    int total = 0;
    for (int pile : piles) total ^= grundy[pile];
    cout << (total ? "WIN" : "LOSE") << '\n';
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    move_count, pile_count = data[0], data[1]
    moves = data[2 : 2 + move_count]
    piles = data[2 + move_count : 2 + move_count + pile_count]
    maximum = max(piles)
    grundy = [0] * (maximum + 1)
    for stones in range(1, maximum + 1):
        reachable = {grundy[stones - move] for move in moves if move <= stones}
        while grundy[stones] in reachable:
            grundy[stones] += 1
    total = 0
    for stones in piles:
        total ^= grundy[stones]
    print("WIN" if total else "LOSE")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Tests that matter

```text
All piles empty.
One pile with no legal move.
Two equal piles, whose equal Grundy values xor to zero.
Move sets that omit 1, so early pile sizes can remain losing.
Many piles with a small maximum size and few piles with a large maximum size.
```

The tiny random oracle runs direct minimax on the complete sorted tuple of pile
sizes, rather than reusing Grundy values. The scale case has `200000` piles and
uses the direct parity property of the one-move set `{1}`.

# What to carry forward

# Complete upsolve notes

## A. Nim Winner
XOR all pile sizes. A zero XOR is losing: every move makes it nonzero. A
nonzero XOR has a move that clears its highest set bit by reducing one pile,
making XOR zero. This is O(n), uses an integer XOR accumulator, and should test
empty-equivalent zero piles, equal piles, and one pile.

## B. Subtraction Game
Let win[s] mean the player to move with s stones can force a win. It is true
iff some legal subtraction reaches a losing state; win[0]=false. Fill upward
through the target. The recurrence is an induction proof, costs
O(target * moves), and must ignore moves larger than s. Test target zero,
move one, and a move set with gaps.

## C. DAG Game
Process vertices in reverse topological order. A vertex is winning iff it has
an edge to a losing successor; sinks are losing. Every successor is already
classified in this order, proving the recurrence. Complexity is O(V+E); test
sinks, disconnected components, and multiple query starts. Use iterative
topological processing in Python for deep graphs.

Run `CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/52_game_theory/check.py` and compare
small subtraction/DAG states with a recursive minimax oracle.

Red-level improvement comes from making the invariant explicit, stress-testing it, and then upsolving the stronger external versions.

## 43. AGC023_F -- 01 on Tree: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc023/tasks/agc023_f?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/43_01_on_tree](problems/43_01_on_tree/README.md)

## Restatement and model

Split `n` distinct people into exactly `k` nonempty teams. Teams are unlabeled:
swapping two whole teams does not make a new partition. Count the partitions
modulo `1,000,000,007`, with `1 <= k <= n <= 2000`.

This is not `k^n`, because that assigns labels to teams and permits empty teams.
It is also not simply `k!` times a value after the fact unless every labeled
assignment uses all teams. We build the count directly by the number of people
and the number of nonempty unlabeled teams.

## Recurrence and trace

Let `S(i,j)` be the number of partitions of the first `i` people into exactly
`j` nonempty teams. Focus on person `i`:

1. They form a singleton team. The first `i-1` people must form `j-1` teams,
   giving `S(i-1,j-1)` choices.
2. They join an existing team. The first `i-1` people form `j` teams, and
   there are `j` teams to join, giving `j*S(i-1,j)` choices.

Thus:

```text
S(i,j) = S(i-1,j-1) + j * S(i-1,j)
S(0,0) = 1
```

For `S(4,2)`:

```text
S(1,1) = 1
S(2,1) = 1,  S(2,2) = 1
S(3,2) = S(2,1) + 2*S(2,2) = 3
S(4,2) = S(3,1) + 2*S(3,2) = 1 + 6 = 7
```

## Algorithm

Use a one-dimensional array where `dp[j]` holds the previous/current row for
`S(_,j)`. Update `j` in decreasing order so `dp[j-1]` still represents the
previous row:

```text
dp[0] = 1
for people from 1 to n:
    for teams from min(people,k) down to 1:
        dp[teams] = dp[teams-1] + teams * dp[teams] modulo MOD
    dp[0] = 0
print dp[k]
```

Setting `dp[0]` to zero after the first row matters: no positive number of
people can be split into zero nonempty teams.

## Correctness proof

Consider any partition of `i` people into `j` nonempty teams. Person `i` is
either alone in their team or is not. In the first case, deleting them leaves
one and only one partition of the first `i-1` people into `j-1` teams. In the
second case, deleting them leaves a partition into `j` teams and records one
of its `j` teams as the one they rejoin. These cases are disjoint and cover all
partitions, proving the recurrence.

The descending update computes exactly that recurrence from the prior row, and
the base `S(0,0)=1` is the unique empty partition. By induction over `people`,
after the final row `dp[k]=S(n,k)`, so the algorithm prints the required count.
QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

The DP takes `O(nk)` time and `O(k)` memory. Multiply in 64-bit before taking
the modulus in C++; Python integers are exact. Test `k=1`, `k=n`, small values
such as `S(4,2)=7`, and a middle-sized `k` where no closed-form shortcut is
available. A common bug is iterating teams upward, which overwrites the
previous-row value needed for `S(i-1,j-1)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1'000'000'007LL;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, k;
    if (!(cin >> n >> k)) return 0;
    vector<long long> dp(k + 1, 0);
    dp[0] = 1;
    for (int people = 1; people <= n; people++) {
        for (int teams = min(people, k); teams >= 1; teams--) {
            dp[teams] = (dp[teams - 1] + teams * dp[teams]) % MOD;
        }
        dp[0] = 0;
    }
    cout << dp[k] << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## A. Catalan Queries
Precompute `C[0]=1` and either the convolution
`C[n]=sum(C[i]*C[n-1-i])` for the local bound or factorial formula under a
legal prime modulus. The first pair decomposition is a bijection, proving the
recurrence. State the actual precompute limit, use long long products, and test
n=0,1,2. A parenthesis enumerator is a small oracle.

## B. Derangement Queries
Use `D[0]=1,D[1]=0,D[n]=(n-1)(D[n-1]+D[n-2])`. Split on whether item one maps
back to its partner or enters a longer cycle; the two cases are disjoint and
complete. Precompute through maximum query in O(maxN), test 0/1/2, and reduce
every product modulo MOD.

## C. Necklace Orbits
Burnside averages fixed colorings: answer is
`inverse(n) * sum_{r=0}^{n-1} k^gcd(n,r)`. A coloring is fixed by rotation r
exactly when it is constant on gcd(n,r) cycles. O(n log n) per local query;
test n=1, prime n, and composite n. Fermat inverse requires the stated prime
modulus and n nonzero modulo it.

Red-level improvement comes from making the invariant explicit, stress-testing it, and then upsolving the stronger external versions.

set partitions, independently of the recurrence. The scale case is a fixed

## 44. AGC023_D -- Go Home: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc023/tasks/agc023_d?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/44_go_home](problems/44_go_home/README.md)

## Restatement and theorem

Given a simple polygon whose vertices have integer coordinates, count lattice
points strictly inside it. Vertices are in boundary order; consecutive collinear
vertices are permitted. Coordinates reach `10^12`, so both cross products and
the total area require `__int128` in C++.

Pick's theorem for a simple lattice polygon states:

```text
area = interior + boundary/2 - 1
2 * interior = double_area - boundary + 2
```

Thus we need exact double area from the shoelace formula and the number of
lattice points on the boundary.

## Boundary count and worked trace

For an edge with displacement `(dx,dy)`, the number of lattice *steps* along
that edge is `gcd(|dx|,|dy|)`. When these values are summed over all cyclic
edges, every polygon vertex is accounted for exactly once, so:

```text
boundary = sum gcd(|x[i+1]-x[i]|, |y[i+1]-y[i]|)
```

For the square `(0,0),(2,0),(2,2),(0,2)`, double area is 8. Each edge has gcd
2, so `boundary=8`. Pick gives:

```text
interior = (8 - 8 + 2) / 2 = 1
```

The unique interior lattice point is `(1,1)`.

## Algorithm

```text
double_area_signed = 0
boundary = 0
for every cyclic edge P -> Q:
    double_area_signed += P.x * Q.y - P.y * Q.x
    boundary += gcd(abs(Q.x-P.x), abs(Q.y-P.y))
double_area = abs(double_area_signed)
print (double_area - boundary + 2) / 2
```

Use the final edge from the last vertex back to the first. The numerator is
always nonnegative and even for a valid simple lattice polygon by Pick's
theorem.

## Correctness proof

The shoelace formula computes the polygon's exact doubled area from its ordered
boundary. For each edge, lattice points on the segment occur at equally spaced
steps of the primitive direction vector; their number of steps is the gcd of
the coordinate differences. Summing gcd values cyclically counts every
boundary lattice point exactly once, including vertices shared by edges.

Therefore the algorithm obtains the exact `double_area` and `boundary` of the
given lattice polygon. Pick's theorem applies because the polygon is simple
and all its vertices are lattice points. Rearranging it gives exactly
`(double_area-boundary+2)/2`, so the printed value is the number of strictly
interior lattice points. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

The algorithm is `O(n)` time and `O(n)` memory if vertices are stored (or
`O(1)` additional memory with streaming). In C++, cast before multiplying and
accumulate in `__int128`; a `long long` product overflows for coordinates near
`10^12`. Python's integers are arbitrary precision. Test a unit-area triangle
with zero interior points, clockwise vertex order, edges with gcd greater than
one, and a polygon with collinear boundary vertices.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Point {
    long long x, y;
};

void print_int128(__int128 value) {
    if (value == 0) {
        cout << 0;
        return;
    }
    string digits;
    while (value > 0) {
        digits.push_back(char('0' + value % 10));
        value /= 10;
    }
    reverse(digits.begin(), digits.end());
    cout << digits;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<Point> polygon(n);
    for (Point& point : polygon) cin >> point.x >> point.y;

    __int128 signed_double_area = 0;
    __int128 boundary = 0;
    for (int index = 0; index < n; index++) {
        Point a = polygon[index];
        Point b = polygon[(index + 1) % n];
        signed_double_area += (__int128)a.x * b.y - (__int128)a.y * b.x;
        boundary += gcd(llabs(b.x - a.x), llabs(b.y - a.y));
    }
    __int128 double_area = signed_double_area >= 0 ? signed_double_area : -signed_double_area;
    __int128 interior = (double_area - boundary + 2) / 2;
    print_int128(interior);
    cout << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import math
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n = data[0]
    polygon = [(data[index], data[index + 1]) for index in range(1, 2 * n + 1, 2)]

    signed_double_area = 0
    boundary = 0
    for index, (x1, y1) in enumerate(polygon):
        x2, y2 = polygon[(index + 1) % n]
        signed_double_area += x1 * y2 - y1 * x2
        boundary += math.gcd(abs(x2 - x1), abs(y2 - y1))
    interior = (abs(signed_double_area) - boundary + 2) // 2
    print(interior)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Compute cross `(bx-ax)*(cy-ay)-(by-ay)*(cx-ax)`. Its sign classifies left,
right, or collinear because it is signed parallelogram area. O(1); use long
long and test all three signs and large coordinates.

## B. Segment Intersection
For closed segments, proper crossing has opposite orientation signs on both
segments; collinear endpoints require inclusive bounding-box `on_segment`.
These cases are complete for two line segments. O(1); test a shared endpoint,

## C. Polygon Double Area
Sum cross products of consecutive vertices including last-to-first, then take
absolute value. Triangulation from the origin proves this signed shoelace sum.
O(n); test clockwise order, a triangle, and a rectangle. Python is exact;
avoid floating point in C++ too.

## 45. ARC069_D -- Flags: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc069/tasks/arc069_d?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/45_flags](problems/45_flags/README.md)

## Restatement and monotonicity

Find the maximum length `L` for which two different starting positions contain
the same length-`L` substring. Overlap is allowed. Comparing every pair of
substrings directly is cubic in the worst case.

Define `possible(L)` to mean that some length-`L` substring occurs twice. This
predicate is monotone: if a repeated substring of length `L` exists, its prefix
of every smaller positive length is also repeated. Therefore binary search can
find the largest true length.

## Hash check for one length

Precompute two polynomial prefix hashes and powers. For every start position,
extract the pair of normalized hashes for its length-`L` substring and insert
the pair into a set. A pair already in the set proves a repeated candidate.

For `banana` and `L=3`, the windows are `ban`, `ana`, `nan`, `ana`; the second
`ana` produces the first duplicate. Since `possible(3)` is true and
`possible(4)` is false, the answer is three.

## Algorithm

```text
precompute two prefix-hash arrays and two power arrays
binary search L from 1 through n:
    scan all length-L windows
    return true as soon as a double-hash pair repeats
print the largest L whose scan returned true
```

The two-modulus hash is probabilistic: a collision could make two unequal
substrings look equal. With independent large prime moduli this risk is
negligible for normal contest use. A suffix array is the deterministic
alternative when the problem requires a proof without that assumption.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** Ignoring hash collisions, `possible(L)` returns true exactly when
a repeated length-`L` substring exists.

**Proof.** The scan inserts the hash of every length-`L` window. Equal
substrings have equal normalized hash pairs, so a second occurrence is found.
Conversely, if no pair repeats, no two windows are equal under collision-free
hashing, so no repeated substring exists.

**Lemma 2.** `possible(L)` is monotone.

**Proof.** If two length-`L` substrings are equal, their first `K` characters
are equal for every `1 <= K <= L`. Thus `possible(L)` implies `possible(K)`.

**Theorem.** Subject to the stated negligible collision probability, the
algorithm prints the longest repeated-substring length.

**Proof.** Lemma 1 evaluates the predicate correctly. Lemma 2 makes its true
lengths an initial interval, so binary search returns its largest member.
That member is exactly the requested maximum length.

## Complexity and implementation notes

One check scans `O(n)` windows; binary search performs `O(log n)` checks, for
`O(n log n)` expected time and `O(n)` memory. Store hash pairs rather than only
one modulus. Normalize a substring using the power for its **length**, not its
right endpoint. The answer may be `0`, and a repeated length `n` is impossible
because there is only one whole-string window.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    string s;
    if (!(cin >> s)) return 0;
    const long long mod1 = 1'000'000'007, mod2 = 1'000'000'009, base = 911'382'323;
    int n = (int)s.size();
    vector<long long> power1(n + 1, 1), power2(n + 1, 1), hash1(n + 1), hash2(n + 1);
    for (int index = 1; index <= n; ++index) {
        power1[index] = power1[index - 1] * base % mod1;
        power2[index] = power2[index - 1] * base % mod2;
        hash1[index] = (hash1[index - 1] * base + s[index - 1]) % mod1;
        hash2[index] = (hash2[index - 1] * base + s[index - 1]) % mod2;
    }
    auto repeated = [&](int length) {
        unordered_set<unsigned long long> seen;
        seen.reserve(2 * (n - length + 1));
        for (int left = 0; left + length <= n; ++left) {
            int right = left + length;
            int first = (hash1[right] - hash1[left] * power1[length] % mod1 + mod1) % mod1;
            int second = (hash2[right] - hash2[left] * power2[length] % mod2 + mod2) % mod2;
            unsigned long long key = (unsigned long long)first * mod2 + second;
            if (!seen.insert(key).second) return true;
        }
        return false;
    };
    int low = 1, high = n, answer = 0;
    while (low <= high) {
        int middle = (low + high) / 2;
        if (repeated(middle)) answer = middle, low = middle + 1;
        else high = middle - 1;
    }
    cout << answer << '\n';
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


MOD1 = 1_000_000_007
MOD2 = 1_000_000_009
BASE = 911_382_323


def main() -> None:
    s = sys.stdin.buffer.readline().strip()
    n = len(s)
    power1 = [1] * (n + 1)
    power2 = [1] * (n + 1)
    hash1 = [0] * (n + 1)
    hash2 = [0] * (n + 1)
    for index, byte in enumerate(s, 1):
        power1[index] = power1[index - 1] * BASE % MOD1
        power2[index] = power2[index - 1] * BASE % MOD2
        hash1[index] = (hash1[index - 1] * BASE + byte) % MOD1
        hash2[index] = (hash2[index - 1] * BASE + byte) % MOD2

    def repeated(length: int) -> bool:
        seen: set[tuple[int, int]] = set()
        for left in range(n - length + 1):
            right = left + length
            key = (
                (hash1[right] - hash1[left] * power1[length]) % MOD1,
                (hash2[right] - hash2[left] * power2[length]) % MOD2,
            )
            if key in seen:
                return True
            seen.add(key)
        return False

    low, high, answer = 1, n, 0
    while low <= high:
        middle = (low + high) // 2
        if repeated(middle):
            answer = middle
            low = middle + 1
        else:
            high = middle - 1
    print(answer)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Tests that matter

```text
One character and all distinct characters: answer 0.
All equal characters: answer n-1.
Overlapping repetitions: banana and aaaaa.
Two long equal blocks at different positions.
Near-equal windows that differ only at their final character.
```

The tiny random oracle compares real slices, not hashes. The scale case is a
200000-character uniform string, which makes every binary-search scan large.

# Complete upsolve notes

## A. Equal Substrings
Build powers and prefix hashes. Normalize each same-length substring hash by
subtracting its preceding prefix times the matching power; equal hashes answer
YES probabilistically. The prefix recurrence proves the extraction formula.
Preprocess O(n), query O(1); double hash in adversarial settings and test
prefix/suffix/full ranges.

## B. Palindrome Substrings
Build the same hash for s and reversed s. Compare `[l,r)` against reversed
`[n-r,n-l)`; equality is the palindrome condition. Preprocess O(n), query
O(1). Test length one, even/odd palindrome, and an off-by-one reverse boundary.

## C. Anagram Substrings
For lowercase input, use 26 prefix counts, not a randomized hash. Two ranges
are anagrams iff every character-count difference agrees. Preprocess O(26n)
or 26 tables and query O(26); test repeated letters, unequal counts, and full
ranges. This is exact and avoids collision reasoning.

In C++ use long long modular multiplication; Python should avoid slicing in the
fast path. Stress all three with direct string comparisons on short random data.

Red-level improvement comes from making the invariant explicit, stress-testing it, and then upsolving the stronger external versions.

## 46. AGC017_F -- Zigzag: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc017/tasks/agc017_f?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/46_zigzag](problems/46_zigzag/README.md)

## Restatement and greedy choice

Choose the largest number of pairwise non-overlapping half-open intervals.
Touching endpoints are compatible, so after choosing `[a,b)`, an interval
`[c,d)` is legal exactly when `c >= b`.

Sort all intervals by increasing finishing time. Scan them in that order and
accept an interval precisely when its start is at least the finish time of the
last accepted interval.

For the sample, the sorted scan accepts `[1,2)`, then `[2,5)`, then `[5,7)`.
The earlier-ending interval `[0,4)` is skipped because it overlaps the chosen
first interval.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma.** After the greedy algorithm chooses its next interval `g`, there is
an optimal schedule whose next interval is `g`.

**Proof.** Consider an optimal schedule compatible with the intervals already
chosen by greedy, and let its next interval be `o`. Greedy chose `g` with the
smallest available end time, so `end(g) <= end(o)`. Replace `o` by `g`: every
later interval of the optimal schedule starts at least `end(o)`, hence also at
least `end(g)`. The replacement remains feasible and has the same size.

**Theorem.** The algorithm returns a maximum-size compatible schedule.

**Proof.** The lemma lets an optimum agree with every greedy choice in turn.
When greedy can no longer accept an interval, neither can an optimum that
agrees with its prefix. Therefore greedy has optimal size.

## Complexity and implementation notes

Sorting costs `O(n log n)` and the scan is `O(n)`, with `O(n)` memory for the
interval list. Sort by end time, not start time or shortest duration. Use
`start >= available_from`, not `>`, because the intervals are half-open.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n;if(!(cin>>n))return 0;vector<pair<long long,long long>> a(n);for(auto& x:a)cin>>x.first>>x.second;sort(a.begin(),a.end(),[](auto x,auto y){return x.second<y.second;});long long available=-1;int answer=0;for(auto [start,end]:a)if(start>=available){++answer;available=end;}cout<<answer<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    intervals = sorted(((data[index], data[index + 1]) for index in range(1, len(data), 2)), key=lambda item: item[1])
    answer = 0
    available_from = -1
    for start, end in intervals:
        if start >= available_from:
            answer += 1
            available_from = end
    print(answer)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Tests that matter

```text
Intervals that touch exactly at endpoints.
Nested intervals, where the shortest one is not necessarily first in input.
Several equal end times.
One interval covering many mutually compatible shorter intervals.
200000 already compatible intervals.
```

The tiny oracle enumerates subsets and checks their sorted compatibility. The
scale case contains 200000 mutually compatible intervals.

## 47. AGC032_E -- Modulo Pairing: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc032/tasks/agc032_e?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/47_modulo_pairing](problems/47_modulo_pairing/README.md)

## Restatement and model

Given a directed acyclic graph, cover every vertex with the smallest possible
number of vertex-disjoint directed paths. A path may have one vertex. There are
at most 2,000 vertices and 10,000 edges, so trying every way to connect paths
is not practical.

Create two copies of every vertex: `u_left` and `u_right`. For each DAG edge
`u -> v`, add bipartite edge `u_left -> v_right`. Matching such an edge means
we put `v` immediately after `u` in one path. Because matching uses each left
and right vertex at most once, no original vertex receives two predecessors or
two successors.

## Trace and count identity

For edges `1->2`, `1->3`, `2->4`, `3->4`, a matching can select `1->2` and
`2->4`. These joins make path `1->2->4`; vertex 3 remains a singleton. There
are four vertices and two selected joins, hence two paths.

Starting from `n` singleton paths, every selected join merges two paths and
reduces the count by one. Therefore a matching of size `M` produces `n-M`
paths. We want as many joins as possible, so the answer is:

```text
minimum path cover = n - maximum bipartite matching
```

The graph must be acyclic. Otherwise the selected joins could form a directed
cycle, which is not a path cover.

## Algorithm

```text
build bipartite adjacency: u_left -> v_right for every original edge u -> v
run augmenting-path matching
print n - matching_size
```

The local limits permit the standard DFS augmenting algorithm. Reset the
visited-right array for every new left-side root so an earlier failed search
does not suppress a valid later reroute.

## Correctness proof

Take any valid path cover with `p` paths. Each path of length `L` contributes
`L-1` consecutive original edges, and all these edges have distinct starts and
distinct ends. They form a matching of size `n-p` in the constructed bipartite
graph. Hence `maximum_matching >= n-p`, so `n-maximum_matching <= p`.

Conversely, take any matching of size `M`. Each matched edge gives an original
edge whose start has at most one selected successor and whose end has at most
one selected predecessor. Thus selected edges form disjoint directed chains;
acyclicity rules out a directed cycle. Add every unmatched vertex as needed as
a singleton chain. These chains cover every vertex and contain exactly `n-M`
paths. Hence an optimal matching gives a path cover of size
`n-maximum_matching`. Together, the two inequalities prove the formula and
the algorithm. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

With DFS augmenting paths, time is `O(n*m)` and memory is `O(n+m)`, suitable
for the stated local bounds. Store the matching by right-side vertex. Test an
edgeless graph (every vertex is a path), a chain (one path), a fork that cannot
put both children after the same parent, and a diamond requiring a rematch.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m;
    if (!(cin >> n >> m)) return 0;
    vector<vector<int>> graph(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
        int from, to;
        cin >> from >> to;
        graph[from - 1].push_back(to - 1);
    }

    vector<int> match_right(n, -1);
    function<bool(int, vector<int>&)> augment = [&](int left, vector<int>& seen) {
        for (int right : graph[left]) {
            if (seen[right]) continue;
            seen[right] = true;
            if (match_right[right] == -1 || augment(match_right[right], seen)) {
                match_right[right] = left;
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    };

    int matching = 0;
    for (int left = 0; left < n; left++) {
        vector<int> seen(n, false);
        matching += augment(left, seen);
    }
    cout << n - matching << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n, m = data[0], data[1]
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    pointer = 2
    for _ in range(m):
        start, end = data[pointer] - 1, data[pointer + 1] - 1
        pointer += 2
        graph[start].append(end)

    match_right = [-1] * n

    def augment(left: int, seen: list[bool]) -> bool:
        for right in graph[left]:
            if seen[right]:
                continue
            seen[right] = True
            if match_right[right] == -1 or augment(match_right[right], seen):
                match_right[right] = left
                return True
        return False

    matching = 0
    for left in range(n):
        matching += augment(left, [False] * n)
    print(n - matching)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10_000)
    main()
```

## 48. AGC005_F -- Many Easy Problems: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc005/tasks/agc005_f?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/48_many_easy_problems](problems/48_many_easy_problems/README.md)

## Restatement and contest interpretation

Each task needs an uninterrupted positive duration and must be completed no
later than its deadline. Tasks run one at a time. Find the maximum number of
tasks that can be completed on time. There are up to 200,000 tasks, so trying
subsets is impossible.

Sorting by deadline is the natural schedule order: for any chosen task set,
earliest-deadline-first is feasible whenever any order is. We will scan in that
order and retain the most valuable resource for maximizing count: short total
time, not a particular task identity.

## Greedy state and trace

Maintain a max-heap of durations of kept tasks and their total duration. For
every task in nondecreasing deadline order, add it. If total duration exceeds
this task's deadline, remove the longest kept task.

For tasks `(duration,deadline)`:

```text
(2,3), (1,3), (3,4), (2,5)
```

the first two fit with total 3. Adding duration 3 gives total 6 beyond deadline
4, so remove duration 3 and retain total 3. Adding the final duration 2 gives
total 5 by deadline 5. Three tasks remain, which is optimal.

Removing the longest duration is crucial. If we removed a shorter task, we
would keep the same number of tasks but leave more occupied time, making all
future deadlines harder to meet.

## Algorithm

```text
sort tasks by deadline
total = 0
kept_durations = empty max-heap
for (duration, deadline) in sorted tasks:
    push duration; total += duration
    if total > deadline:
        total -= largest duration in heap
        pop that duration
print heap size
```

Only one removal is needed per task: before adding, the kept set fits the
previous deadline, which is no larger than the current one. Removing a duration
at least as large as the newly added duration returns total to a feasible value.

## Correctness proof

After processing any deadline prefix, maintain that the heap is a feasible
maximum-cardinality selection from that prefix and, among selections of that
cardinality, has minimum total duration. Initially this is true.

When a task is added without exceeding its deadline, the heap gains one task
and is feasible. A larger cardinality was impossible in the previous prefix,
so this is maximum. When adding causes an overflow, no feasible selection with
one extra task can exist: such a selection must include the new task (the old
prefix could not contain that many), and the induction hypothesis gives the
smallest possible total duration among the required old task count. Removing
the largest duration leaves the smallest total duration among choices of the
old cardinality, restoring the invariant.

For a selected set, deadline order makes every completion prefix no later than
the corresponding processed deadline; the invariant's feasibility therefore
means all kept tasks can be scheduled on time. At the end its cardinality is
maximum, so the printed heap size is the answer. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

Sorting and heap updates take `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` memory. Use `long
long` for accumulated duration and deadlines in C++; Python integers are safe.
Test all tasks individually impossible, equal deadlines, a long early task that
must be replaced by several short ones, and one task. A common error is using a
min-heap, which discards the wrong task.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<pair<long long, long long>> tasks;
    tasks.reserve(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        long long duration, deadline;
        cin >> duration >> deadline;
        tasks.push_back({deadline, duration});
    }
    sort(tasks.begin(), tasks.end());

    priority_queue<long long> kept;
    long long total = 0;
    for (auto [deadline, duration] : tasks) {
        kept.push(duration);
        total += duration;
        if (total > deadline) {
            total -= kept.top();
            kept.pop();
        }
    }
    cout << kept.size() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import heapq
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n = data[0]
    tasks = [(data[index + 1], data[index]) for index in range(1, 2 * n + 1, 2)]
    tasks.sort()

    kept: list[int] = []  # Negative durations make Python's min-heap a max-heap.
    total = 0
    for deadline, duration in tasks:
        heapq.heappush(kept, -duration)
        total += duration
        if total > deadline:
            total += heapq.heappop(kept)
    print(len(kept))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## 49. AGC024_F -- Simple Subsequence Problem: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc024/tasks/agc024_f?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/49_simple_subsequence_problem](problems/49_simple_subsequence_problem/README.md)

## Restatement and objectives

One team works on one problem at a time. Problem `i` needs `time[i]` minutes;
the contest lasts `limit` minutes. Choose and order problems so that as many as
possible finish by the limit. Among schedules with the maximum number solved,
minimize the total penalty: the sum of their completion times.

There can be 200,000 problems. The two objectives matter in that order: never
sacrifice a solved problem merely to lower penalty.

## Greedy choice and trace

Sort durations increasingly. Take them while their running sum remains within
the limit. For durations `[3,1,2,2]` and limit 5, sorted durations are
`[1,2,2,3]`. The first three fit, with completion times `1,3,5`, hence:

```text
solved = 3
penalty = 1 + 3 + 5 = 9
```

The fourth duration cannot fit. No set of four can fit because the sorted first
four are already the four smallest durations. Among the three selected tasks,
doing a longer one before a shorter one can only increase the completion-time
sum.

## Algorithm

```text
sort all durations increasingly
elapsed = penalty = solved = 0
for duration in sorted durations:
    if elapsed + duration > limit:
        break
    elapsed += duration
    penalty += elapsed
    solved += 1
print solved, penalty
```

All durations are positive. Once the next sorted duration fails, every
remaining duration is at least as large and also fails.

## Correctness proof

For any `k`, the sum of the `k` smallest durations is no larger than the sum
of any other `k` durations. Therefore if the greedy algorithm cannot fit the
first `k` sorted tasks, no schedule can complete `k` tasks within the limit;
and whenever it fits them, those tasks themselves form a feasible schedule.
The number selected by the greedy algorithm is thus the maximum possible solved
count.

Now fix any selected set. If two consecutive scheduled tasks have durations
`a > b`, their contribution to the two completion times is `(P+a)+(P+a+b)`.
Swapping them gives `(P+b)+(P+b+a)`, smaller by `a-b`, without changing any
later completion time. Repeatedly swapping inversions gives nondecreasing
duration order with minimum penalty. The greedy schedule uses exactly that
order, so among maximum-count schedules it has minimum total penalty. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

Sorting costs `O(n log n)` time and storage is `O(n)`. Use `long long` for
elapsed time and penalty in C++; the penalty can exceed a 32-bit integer. Test
no feasible problem, exact fit, repeated durations, and input ordered from
longest to shortest. A frequent contest mistake is sorting only after selecting
an arbitrary feasible set, which can lose the primary objective.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n;
    long long limit;
    if (!(cin >> n >> limit)) return 0;
    vector<long long> durations(n);
    for (long long& duration : durations) cin >> duration;
    sort(durations.begin(), durations.end());

    long long elapsed = 0;
    long long penalty = 0;
    int solved = 0;
    for (long long duration : durations) {
        if (elapsed + duration > limit) break;
        elapsed += duration;
        penalty += elapsed;
        solved++;
    }
    cout << solved << ' ' << penalty << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n, limit = data[0], data[1]
    durations = sorted(data[2 : 2 + n])
    elapsed = 0
    penalty = 0
    solved = 0
    for duration in durations:
        if elapsed + duration > limit:
            break
        elapsed += duration
        penalty += elapsed
        solved += 1
    print(solved, penalty)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## 50. AGC016_F -- Games on DAG: local companion

Official AtCoder task: <https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc016/tasks/agc016_f?lang=en>
Local package: [problems/50_games_on_dag](problems/50_games_on_dag/README.md)

## State expansion

The free-edge coupon is part of the route history. Reaching the same vertex
before and after using it are different situations, so use states `(vertex,used)`
where `used` is zero or one. From `(v,used)`, an edge of weight `w` gives
`(to,used)` at cost `w`; when `used=0`, it also gives `(to,1)` at cost zero.

All expanded-edge costs are nonnegative, so run Dijkstra from `(1,0)`. The
answer is the smaller distance to `(n,0)` and `(n,1)`.

## Correctness proof

Every legal original route maps to exactly one expanded path by marking whether
its coupon has already been used. Its expanded cost equals its paid cost.
Conversely, every expanded path uses at most one zero-cost coupon transition,
so it maps to a legal route of the same cost. Dijkstra returns shortest paths
in this nonnegative expanded graph; therefore the reported minimum is optimal.

## Complexity and tests

The expanded graph has `2n` states and at most `4m` directed transitions, so
Dijkstra costs `O((n+m) log n)` time and `O(n+m)` memory. Test one edge (answer
zero), a route where the most expensive edge is not on the ordinary shortest
path, and a long chain. The tiny oracle uses repeated edge relaxation on both
coupon layers; the scale case is a 200000-vertex chain.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n,m;if(!(cin>>n>>m))return 0;vector<vector<pair<int,long long>>>g(n);while(m--){int a,b;long long w;cin>>a>>b>>w;--a;--b;g[a].push_back({b,w});g[b].push_back({a,w});}const long long I=4e18;vector<vector<long long>>d(2,vector<long long>(n,I));priority_queue<array<long long,3>,vector<array<long long,3>>,greater<array<long long,3>>>q;d[0][0]=0;q.push({0,0,0});while(!q.empty()){auto[x,u,v]=q.top();q.pop();if(x!=d[u][v])continue;for(auto[to,w]:g[v]){if(x+w<d[u][to])d[u][to]=x+w,q.push({x+w,u,to});if(!u&&x<d[1][to])d[1][to]=x,q.push({x,1,to});}}cout<<min(d[0][n-1],d[1][n-1])<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys,heapq
def main():
 d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
 if not d:return
 n,m=d[:2];g=[[] for _ in range(n)];i=2
 for _ in range(m):
  a,b,w=d[i]-1,d[i+1]-1,d[i+2];i+=3;g[a].append((b,w));g[b].append((a,w))
 inf=10**30;dist=[[inf]*n for _ in range(2)];dist[0][0]=0;pq=[(0,0,0)]
 while pq:
  cost,used,v=heapq.heappop(pq)
  if cost!=dist[used][v]:continue
  for to,w in g[v]:
   if cost+w<dist[used][to]:dist[used][to]=cost+w;heapq.heappush(pq,(cost+w,used,to))
   if not used and cost<dist[1][to]:dist[1][to]=cost;heapq.heappush(pq,(cost,1,to))
 print(min(dist[0][-1],dist[1][-1]))
if __name__=='__main__':main()
```
